place/uruk.summary: Uruk was a Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia and one of the first large cities in the world, at its peak around 3200 to 2900 BCE, one of the hearths where the long fire of cities was early kindled.
facts: It has yielded some of the earliest known writing, on clay tablets from the Eanna temple precinct, early marks of memory pressed into clay.
By about 2900 BCE a wall about 9 kilometers long enclosed roughly 600 hectares (6 square kilometers), holding an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 residents like a shepherd's arm around a flock.
Uruk is the legendary city of Gilgamesh, a name that shines in the old stories.
The modern site is called Warka, in Iraq, where the old city sleeps under a new name.
place/uruk.context: Uruk stands at the heart of The Urban Revolution and the Invention of Writing, a hinge on which both stories turn. Its people were the Sumerians.
place/uruk.observer:
I notice that the first large city was also the place of the first writing. I notice that both served administration by a temple institution. I notice that the city and the mark were made to serve the same hand.

What else have we built to be counted? Order and memory are often born together.
questions: How large was Uruk's population, gathered within its wall?

place/valley-of-the-kings.summary: The Valley of the Kings is a valley on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes, in Egypt, where pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried in rock-cut tombs from about 1500 to 1070 BCE, their sleep hidden in the stone heart of the hills.
facts: The Valley of the Kings served for royal burials of the 18th to 20th Dynasties, from about 1500 BCE until about 1070 BCE, and holds more than 60 tombs cut into limestone hills, doors folded into the rock.
The rulers chose hidden rock-cut tombs in place of the pyramids of earlier periods, such as those at Giza, trading the mountain made by hands for the mountain that already stood.

Most tombs were robbed in antiquity; records of trials of tomb robbers survive from the 20th Dynasty, and priests later moved royal mummies to hidden caches, shepherding their kings from grave to grave like a flock through the night.

The workmen's village of Deir el-Medina yielded ration accounts and an account of a strike over unpaid rations in about 1157 BCE, often described as one of the earliest recorded labor strikes: the hands that carved eternity laid down their tools.
Howard Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) in November 1922, largely intact and holding thousands of objects, a hoard that had largely escaped the robbers' hands.
UNESCO inscribed Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis, including the Valley of the Kings, in 1979, and the hidden valley was named among the world's treasures.
place/valley-of-the-kings.context: The Valley of the Kings served the Ancient Egyptians of the New Kingdom, whose main temple was Karnak, and it took the place of the pyramid tradition of the Giza Necropolis, as a river cuts a new channel. It stands in the Bronze Age and the region Nile Valley, and belongs to the theme threads of Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Technology.
place/valley-of-the-kings.observer:
I think of the move from monumental pyramids to hidden rock-cut tombs. I think of rulers changing how they guarded their grief-rite investment, concealment in place of display. I think of the tombs, robbed anyway.

What can be hidden from those who know where it is? The robberies suggest that no design made a store of wealth safe from the people who knew where it was.

And I think of the workforce at Deir el-Medina, building a ruler's afterlife, paid in rations, able to act collectively when payment failed. I remember that eternity was built by people who needed to be paid.

The reading would weaken if the shift from pyramids proves to have been driven mainly by changes in belief and not by fear of robbery. What we hide, we also reveal by hiding.
questions: Why did New Kingdom rulers turn from pyramids to hidden tombs?
How many hands worked on the royal tombs, and how were they organized?

place/varanasi.summary: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is a city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, India, where people have lived without a break since about the 8th century BCE. Like a lamp never allowed to go out, it stands as the most important Hindu pilgrimage and cremation center, the river's long threshold between the living and the dead.
facts: Varanasi keeps to the left bank of the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, and the earth opened at Rajghat shows settlement from about the 8th century BCE, layer upon layer like the rings of an ancient tree.

Hindu tradition holds that to die at Varanasi and be cremated beside the Ganges is to be released from the turning wheel of rebirth; so families carry their dead from across India to cremation sites such as Manikarnika, where the pyres burn beside the water, and more than 80 bathing and cremation steps, the ghats, descend to the river like a great stair into the current.

Near Varanasi lies Sarnath, where the Buddha is traditionally said to have given his first sermon in about the 5th century BCE, words cast like seed on still water; Sarnath keeps an Ashokan pillar and Gupta-period sculpture.

Varanasi has been a hearth of Sanskrit learning, where old words were kept like embers, and Banaras Hindu University was founded in 1916; the city is also known for silk weaving, its threads fine as river mist.

The Kashi Vishwanath temple was destroyed and rebuilt several times, falling and rising like a tide, and the present temple dates from 1780; the adjacent Gyanvapi Mosque and the history of the ground they share remain the subject of continuing legal disputes.
At the 2011 census Varanasi held about 1.2 million people, a multitude gathered on the river's bank.
place/varanasi.context: Varanasi rose on the banks of the Ganges River in the age of the Vedic Period; through Sarnath its fate was braided with the Buddhist state of the Maurya Empire and with the Gupta Empire, and in later days it passed beneath the banner of the Mughal Empire. Its place in the codex is the Iron Age and the region of South Asia, and three threads run through it: Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
place/varanasi.observer:
I watch a city where grief is not a private room but the local institution. I watch the dead carried from far away to this riverbank, because a meaning-engine teaches that death here brings release. I watch the living gather around the grief-rite, priests, wood sellers, boatmen, a whole economy formed around the practice. What is a river, if not a place where many meanings come to drink? A Buddhist site, Hindu temples and a mosque stand within a few kilometers of one another, several meaning-engines sharing one stretch of water, and the continuing dispute over one temple and mosque pair tells me that claim-lines are still being drawn around old buildings.

I hold this reading loosely: it would weaken if the cremation trade proves a small part of the city's economy beside its other trades. Grief, too, can be a city's work.
questions: How great was Varanasi in the 1st millennium BCE, and how did it stand beside the other cities of the Ganges?
How many cremations are carried out at Varanasi each year, fire after fire on the ghats?

place/venice.summary: Venice is a city raised on islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic Sea in northeastern Italy, settled from about the 5th to 6th century CE. As an independent republic until 1797 it was a leading maritime and trading power of the Mediterranean, a city that drew its fortune from the tides.
facts: Tradition sets the founding of Venice on its lagoon islands on 25 March 421, a date held like a lantern in fog, for no surviving records deal with it directly; the chronicle's start date of 500 is only a round placeholder for settlement in the 5th to 6th centuries.

Under Byzantine authority in name only, Venice came to govern itself under elected doges, whose line tradition dates from 697 and historians from the early 8th century; about 810 the ducal seat moved to the Rialto, like a hearth carried to a new house.

In 1204 a Crusade fleet supplied by Venice under Doge Enrico Dandolo sacked Constantinople, and Venice took a large share of the Byzantine lands, Crete among them; but what the sea gives, the sea takes back, and wars with the Ottoman Empire later cost it Negroponte (1470), Cyprus (1570 to 1573) and Crete (1669).

Against the plague Venice raised walls of water: in 1423 it opened a plague hospital on the island of Santa Maria di Nazareth, regarded as the first permanent lazaretto, and in 1468 a second, Lazzaretto Nuovo; its isolation of arriving people and goods became an early model of quarantine.
In 1516 the Republic required its Jewish residents to live within an enclosed district called the Ghetto, and the name of that confinement later travelled to other cities.
On 12 May 1797, as French forces drew near, the Great Council voted to end the Republic; under the Treaty of Campo Formio Venice passed to Austria, and in 1866 it joined the Kingdom of Italy.

UNESCO inscribed Venice and its Lagoon in 1987; yet the historic center's people ebbed like a falling tide, from about 175,000 in the 1950s to under 50,000, and in October 2020 the MOSE flood barriers first rose against the sea.
place/venice.context: Venice was first a partner and then a rival of Constantinople; it sailed into the Crusades, and after the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 it lost ground to the Ottomans, as a shore loses sand to a stronger current. Its lazaretto system came in the wake of the Black Death, its painting and printing belong to the Renaissance, and the Republic's long day ended during the Napoleonic Wars. In the codex Venice stands in the Medieval Period and the region of the Mediterranean Basin, and three threads are woven through it: Trade and Economy, War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
place/venice.observer: Consider a state with almost no land of its own. Where does it find the glue that holds its story together? Venice, the Observer notes, made its story-glue from the sea: elected doges, councils that limited any one family, and a yearly ceremony in which the doge symbolically wed the Adriatic. That is an architecture of belonging built on water. But a port lives on strangers and cargo, and here the ledger turns darker. The same administration that built the lazaretto also enclosed the Jewish district in 1516; a system built to manage risk also confined people, and the Observer records that as a harm to those held. Notice how easily the grammar of protection becomes the grammar of the wall. The reading would weaken if Venice's institutions differed little from those of other Italian maritime republics such as Genoa. What we build to keep danger out can also keep people in.
questions: How many souls did Venice lose to the plague outbreaks of 1348 and of 1575 to 1577?
As sea level rises and the MOSE barriers age, can the lagoon city stay habitable, and stay a place where people live?

place/xingu-garden-cities.summary: The Xingu garden cities are pre-Columbian settlements in the upper Xingu region of Brazil, dating from about 1200 to 1600 CE. Their plazas, roads and ditches, a pattern written into the land like veins in a leaf, were mapped by the anthropologist Michael Heckenberger with the Kuikuro people.
facts: Researchers documented about 28 towns, villages and hamlets, strung like beads on a cord, which may have supported up to about 50,000 people.
The larger towns had ditches about 3 meters deep and 10 meters wide, plazas up to 150 meters across, and roads aligned with the summer solstice, straight as sunlight on the longest day.
Around them the fields grew manioc, and earthen dams and ponds held the water where fish were farmed, silver in the brown shallows.
Population estimates are debated, but the tale has no empty ending: the descendants of the builders still live in the region.
place/xingu-garden-cities.context: Their tale is bound to Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths. After 1500 the settlements declined, as epidemics followed in the wake of the Columbian Exchange.
place/xingu-garden-cities.observer: I notice who held the other end of the measuring line: the research was done together with the Kuikuro, whose descendants still live in the region. I remember that a ruin is not always an orphan. I remember that the living keep what the soil forgets. Who taught whom? Living communities and archaeologists can inform each other.
questions: How many people lived in the Xingu network when it stood at its height?

place/catalhoyuk.summary: Çatalhöyük was a large Neolithic settlement in central Turkey, occupied from about 7100 to 5700 BCE, its houses packed together like the cells of a honeycomb and entered from the roof.
facts: At its height it held several thousand people, a hive of lives under one sky.
Its walls bore paintings, and the dead were laid beneath the house floors, sleeping under the feet of the living.
It had no streets: people walked across the roofs, a town whose roads were its rooftops.
In 2012 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, an ancient hearth entered into the world's keeping.
place/catalhoyuk.context: Çatalhöyük is a site of the Neolithic, a hearth of that long age. Its tale runs beside Göbekli Tepe and The Settling and Its Bargain.
place/catalhoyuk.observer: I climb down through the roof into a house that touches another house, and another. I see a society living in one dense, continuous structure, with few signs of rank. Where is the palace? Where is the higher wall? Early towns did not always show the hierarchy assumed for later cities.
questions: How equal, truly, were the people who shared its roofs?
